title: Nano Banana 2 Is Coming to Google Earth
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 30, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google Earth is getting a Nano Banana 2 upgrade.
                                            With it, you can create futuristic vistas or dive back into the historic past of a place.
                                            The update is rolling out now for all Google Earth users on the web.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Known by the codename Nano Banana 2, the most recent AI image generation updates added to Google Gemini have been a significant step forward in terms of quality and accuracy, and now similar capabilities are being plugged into the Google Earth app on the web. It means you're able to use the aerial, satellite, and 3D imagery packed into Google Earth as the basis for prompts for AI images—maybe peering into the distant past with a historical reconstruction or looking to the future with a sci-fi reimagining.We've already seen just how precise and realistic the Nano Banana-powered features in Google Gemini are now, and Google has five suggestions for how you might deploy these capabilities in Google Earth. First, you can learn while exploring, so maybe getting the AI to build an infographic on the Statue of Liberty with key historical facts about it.
    
            
            One idea for the new feature: Infographics (the Statue of Liberty in this case).
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
A text prompt such as "reimagine this empty lot in Tokyo as a vibrant shopping and retail district with open spaces" would transform a rather bare part of the Google Earth 3D map into something quite different. You can also visualize personal projects such as a dream lakeside home or an extension for your current property. Google Earth would combine the existing landscape with whatever you prompted, and help you come up with ideas as part of the planning stage.
You can also look forwards and backwards. "Sometimes it’s fun to let your imagination run wild," says Google, suggesting that you might want to get the AI to imagine how a place might look in a hundred years. (It might be worth nudging your prompt towards a utopian rather than dystopian vision of the future.)Finally, Google suggests you dive back into the past. The company showcased a demo with the prompt "render a hyper-realistic view of what these Pompeii ruins looked like in 78 AD," which could be used by teachers, for example. That would instantly transform today's ruins "into a bustling, colorful street scene from the Roman Empire," in Google's words.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
These new features come with the usual AI image caveats, however. While Nano Banana 2 can pull real-world information and images from the web, and is able to render graphics with more consistency and accuracy than previous models, there's still going to be the usual weaknesses involved with AI: Your lakeside home might not be entirely structurally sound, and the Pompeii reconstruction may not be entirely authentic—so bear that in mind when your images are produced.
    
            
            Pompeii in all its original glory, as depicted by AI. 
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
When I asked Google about this, a representative emphasized the real-world knowledge base that Nano Banana 2 draws on, which includes all the text and graphics it can find online, as well as the vast number of images that have been plugged into the AI during its training. With Google Earth, it will also trace over the structure ruins that are still in place when it comes to Pompeii, for example.For a bit more clarity, you can try quizzing the Nano Banana 2 model inside the main Gemini app: I got it to render an imagined scene from Pompeii just prior to it being smothered by Vesuvius, then asked about the image accuracy. The AI said it had combined a bunch of real, historical information points to render the scene, including details on Pompeii's raised sidewalks, and the clothing styles of the day. Google hasn't said anything specific about usage limits, but the Nano Banana 2 upgrade is rolling out now globally, for all users of Google Earth on the web.

title: You Might Soon Have to Pay More for Higher Access to Siri AI
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 31, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Justin Sullivan / Staff via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Siri AI and Apple Intelligence can be demanding on Apple's servers. As such, you may have to pay more for better access.
                                            Outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook said that the company expects people to use these features "a lot."
                                            As such, Apple "will have some kind of upgrade possibilities on iCloud+ where people can buy up the stack."
                                            We don't know what that looks like at this time, but you may need to pay an additional fee on top of your iCloud+ plan for higher access.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        When your compatible iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Apple Watch update to the "27" era later this year, you'll notice a huge upgrade to your digital assistant. Siri is now "Siri AI," and, through the assistance of Apple Intelligence, can now do a lot more than the previous Siri could. While that means your assistant can now answer questions regarding what's on your screen and provide responses similar to ChatGPT, I'm personally hoping the simple commands are more reliable. (Please stop checking my contacts for the weather, Siri.)The results from the second round of Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game are in! See what Lifehacker readers think Apple will announce later this year, and tune in for round three starting Aug. 18 for your chance to win the latest Apple Watch.The best of Siri AI may cost youYou might be excited to try out Apple's take on ChatGPT and Gemini, and Apple knows it. During Apple's earnings call on Thursday, outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that he thinks people will want to take advantage of Siri AI and Apple's new AI features "a lot." AI, of course, puts a huge demand on system resources. If your Siri AI use is on-device, that burden is placed solely on your iPhone, Mac, or iPad. But Siri AI isn't entirely on-device: Plenty of its features need to outsource processing power to the cloud in order to function. The more customers use Apple's AI programs and tap into the company's cloud servers, the more expensive it is for Apple to maintain those systems. 
Tim Cook has a solution here. In the earnings calls, Cook said, "we will have some kind of upgrade possibilities on iCloud+ where people can buy up the stack." Cook didn't elaborate, but it's clear where this is headed: Apple, like other tech companies, will let you pay more to access higher usage limits and, potentially, prioritized processing speeds. This isn't entirely a surprise. When Apple officially announced Siri AI and its newest Apple Intelligence features, the company did mention that there would be usage limits on some of its most demanding processes—including, notably, image generation. Image Playground, Apple's AI image generator, is supposed to get a big upgrade this year, and that apparently won't come free of charge. This is the first time Apple has acknowledged that Siri AI may be paywalled in some way, shape, or form. At the time, Apple said "increased access is available with most iCloud+ subscription plans." That could still be the case, and most iCloud+ users could access Siri AI as part of their plan—or you may have to upgrade your plan further to access those best usage limits. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
While most Apple users likely won't want to pay for more Siri AI and Apple Intelligence access—plenty of us refuse to pay for iCloud storage, after all—there will undoubtedly be users who will try it out. It would be just one more perk Apple can advertise to add to its revenue stream, which is proving to be quite lucrative indeed. As The Verge highlights, the company posted $30.74 billion in revenue from services alone. If Apple can make more money from users interested in pushing Siri AI to its limits, all the better.   We don't know how much these usage limits will costThat said, we don't know what Apple plans to charge here. At this time, iCloud+ plans range from the following: 50GB: $0.99200GB: $2.992TB: $9.996TB: $29.9912TB: $59.99Will each plan come with its own pricing tier for added usage limits? Will Apple simply lock higher usage limits to its more premium plans? Maybe 200GB subscribers will need to bump up to $4.99 per month for higher usage limits, which would match Google's basic AI Plus price. Until Apple releases more details, we just don't know for sure.

title: It Just Got a Lot Cheaper to Try Gemini Spark, Google's AI Agent
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Gemini Spark, the AI agent built into Google Gemini, is now a lot cheaper to try out in the U.S. Previously, Gemini Spark was exclusive to the Google AI Ultra plan, which costs $100-$200 per month. The company is now bringing the agentic AI to its AI Pro plan, which costs $20 per month. (For now, this change is exclusive to the U.S.)When Gemini Spark was announced during Google I/O 2026, its features seemed potentially useful, but the barrier to entry was too high for most people. That appears to be changing now, as Google has cut the price by as much as 90%. It is not yet available on the $5/month AI Plus plan or the free tier, but that could change in the future too—though it's likely that using Gemini Spark on lower pricing tiers could mean that you hit your usage limits much faster.What is Gemini Spark?Google Gemini is a chatbot and a voice assistant that answers your questions, creates text, media, and even entire apps for you. Gemini Spark takes those capabilities to your Google account and executes actions for you.
You can think of Gemini Spark as a personal AI assistant that can look at your emails, calendar entries, photos, and other data in your Google account to perform tasks on your behalf. You can use Spark to bulk unsubscribe from mailing lists, make flight bookings, send reminder emails to clients, colleagues, or family members, book appointments, and much more. Having said all that, a Gemini Spark overview from out sister site PC Mag emphasizes that its features tend to overlap with Gemini. PC Mag called Spark the best AI agent yet, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Does Gemini Spark respect your privacy?To someone who is even remotely privacy-conscious, using Gemini Spark is going to sound quite invasive: You basically have to give it access to your entire computer if you want it to be able to act on your behalf. Google is aware of that, and has programmed the AI agent to ask for confirmations before performing certain actions. If you ask the agent to find birthday photos from 2017 and email them to someone, for example, Gemini Spark will show you the pictures and ask for a confirmation before actually sending the email. It applies the same logic to deleting emails, sending messages, using your saved credit cards to pay for reservations, and more.It's worth keeping in mind that AI services have created serious problems for people who use these apps without due caution. The biggest strength of Gemini is its access to all the data that’s in your Google account, but if you give it unrestricted access and the AI agent messes up a request, you could be stuck with an incorrect hotel reservation, a flight booked to a wrong country, or other serious consequences.

title: This App Is (Sort of) Bringing Back Samsung Messages
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 29, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Karlis Dambrans via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            "Messages by OzarksMade" recreates the experience of Samsung Messages, but this time with RCS.
                                            The app arrives after Samsung shut down its proprietary messaging app earlier this month.
                                            Messages by OzarksMade is currently in beta, and any interested users can try it for free.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Earlier this month, Samsung officially killed off its proprietary messaging app. It wasn't much of a surprise. The company had announced the end of Samsung Messages back in April, and, before that, had slowly distanced itself from the app by keeping it off new Galaxy phones by default. If you have a newer Galaxy phone, it's possible you didn't even use Samsung Messages at the time of deprecation. But for legacy users, the app's retirement was sad and frustrating, as the only viable option to retain features and message history is Google Messages—a fine enough chat app, but yet another Google product Galaxy users must rely on. As reported by Android Authority, app developer OzarksMade wants to continue Samsung Messages' legacy. Rather than keep the original app running, OzarksMade created a new messaging app that mimics the look and feel of Samsung Messages: Messages by OzarksMade. The new app is designed with both Samsung Messages and One UI in mind: To the untrained eye, not only does this look like a Samsung Galaxy app, it looks like Samsung Messages.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: OzarksMade
                    
    
Messages by OzarksMade also adds RCS support in the app. There is a catch, however: While you can send and receive RCS messages in Messages by OzarksMade, you'll need to tap into Google Messages via Messages by OzarksMade's "Companion Mode." You won't have to use Google Messages itself, but it will be powering RCS in the new app. You don't have to use Companion Mode, and can eschew Google Messages altogether, but you will be limited to SMS and MMS—the true Samsung Messages experience.
While you should be mindful of making any new chat app your default messaging provider, OzarksMade does say that all messages remain on-device, so it shouldn't store your texts on its servers. In addition, OzarksMade says it takes anonymous information for statistics purposes only, including "a random identifier that is generated on your device, the app's version and release channel, your device model, and your Android version." However, as Android Authority points out, this app closely resembles Samsung's own products, and the company may seek to shut the app down should it feel OzarksMade infringed on any copyrights.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to try Messages by OzarksMadeThis new app isn't out just yet, as it will launch on Thursday, Aug. 13. If you're interested, you'll need to join Messages by OzarksMade's beta, which is currently ongoing. To start, join the app's Google Group with the same Google account you use on your phone. Once you're in, you'll be able to see Messages by OzarksMade's Play Store page here. The developer says the Play Store will list the app at $0.99, but since you've joined the Google Group, you'll see an option called "Test Card, always approves" after tapping the payment. By choosing this option, you'll be able to download the app for free. If you don't see this option, you didn't properly sign up for the Google Group, and you'll need to try again.

title: Scammers Are Impersonating Spotify to Steal Your Credit Card Info
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 28, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: 	Chris McGrath / Getty Images News via Getty Inages
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Scammers love to impersonate trusted brands—ranging from big tech names like Microsoft and Google to password managers and payment apps—in their phishing campaigns to lure their marks, and their latest guise is Spotify. A new email is circulating alerting users to supposed payment issues, prompting them to hand over their credit card details and Spotify login credentials. Phishing emails use Spotify brandingAs The Guardian reports, Spotify users have received messages with the subject line "review billing info" claiming that the platform "encountered an issue while processing your recent payment." Recipients are urged to "review and update" their information to keep their accounts active. The button in the email directs users to a spoofed website, where users are prompted to enter their username and password, followed by their credit card number, address, and phone number—everything scammers need to make fraudulent purchases. One victim reported seeing a suspicious charge for more than $600 within minutes of handing over their information. The emails closely replicate Spotify's branding, including its colors and logo, and appear to come from a sender called MySpotify. The fraudulent website also looks convincing at first glance. However, unlike some of the more sophisticated phishing schemes that exploit vulnerabilities in order to use real domains (like Google and PayPal), this one from Spotify breaks down when you look closer. 
For one, both the sender's address and the website URL clearly are not connected to spotify.com or any legitimate subdomain. The subject line is all lowercase, and there are no specifics about users' subscriptions or accounts in the email body. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to avoid getting scammed by Spotify impersonatorsPayment issues are a common scam tactic, and you should always be skeptical of any communication that urges you to provide or update banking or credit card info (or sends you to a login page along the way, which is designed to harvest your credentials). If you receive a notification from Spotify about failed payments, don't click links, download attachments, or reply. Spotify won't request payment info, passwords, or other sensitive information over email.If you're concerned about a payment or subscription problem, go directly to your account in the Spotify app or a web browser instead. If you've already entered your Spotify credentials into a suspicious site, change your password and keep an eye on your credit card transactions to catch any fraudulent charges. You can also forward phishing emails to [email protected].

    Table of Contents
    
        
        If your phone isn't working, it's not just you: T-Mobile is down. The posts allegedly come from multiple states, including Utah, Arizona, Missouri, Michigan, and Illinois, indicating a potential nationwide outage. T-Mobile has not made a public comment about the outage so far, but its Help account on X is responding to user complaints with boilerplate responses. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    

T-Mobile isn't the only carrier to experience a notable outage this year. Back in January, Verizon was hit with a major nationwide outage. The company claimed the outage did not stem from a cyberattack, rather a software issue. We don't know why T-Mobile is down at the moment, but, in all likelihood, the company will update the public sooner than later, if not fix the issue altogether.

title: Google Docs Is Rolling Out These Three New Gemini Features
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 30, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google is rolling out new Gemini features in Google Docs for select users.
                                            Gemini can now generate and edit images directly in Google Docs, pulling from the context of your doc.
                                            Gemini can also generate and edit multiple images at once, based on the prompt.
                                            The features are rolling out now to Workspace users, including Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subcribers.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Google makes both Gemini and Docs, so it's not surprising that you'll find plenty of the former's features while using the latter. Gemini has a ton of Google Docs integration, including reading your text out loud, searching and summarizing your Docs in Drive, and a "Gemini bar" embedded into the app for prompting anytime. It's to the point that it's tough to avoid, which isn't great news for Google Docs users uninterested in AI features. Of course, that won't stop Google. The company continues to add new Gemini features at a steady clip, and this week is no exception. As Android Authority notes, Gemini is now rolling out new image creation and editing abilities available directly in Google Docs. Google announced the changes in a Workspace update on Tuesday, highlighting how Docs users can tap into Gemini to create and edit images, diagrams, and infographics in their documents. According to Google, Gemini has three new functions Workspace users can take advantage of. First, users can create infographics or diagrams that summarize the doc in question. You could ask Gemini to do something like "add a diagram that explains the proposal at the top of this doc," or "create an infographic that summarizes the doc visually." Google says Gemini will pull from the context of the doc for these graphics, so these images should reflect what you have written in your doc—excluding the odd hallucination, of course.
In addition, Gemini can "refine existing visuals." You can ask Gemini to adjust the images in your doc with requests like, "change the aspect ratio of this image to 4:3," or "match the image's style to the other images in this doc." Finally, you can also ask Gemini to generate or edit multiple images at once. You could request the AI to create infographics in each section of your doc, or update all images at once.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Who has access to these new Gemini features?These new additions to Google Docs aren't rolling out to everyone. Instead, they're exclusive to Workspace users, which includes Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. If you pay for Google's AI features, you can try these out once they roll out on your end. If your school, work, or organization uses Workspace, the same applies. Here's the full list:Business: Business Standard and PlusEnterprise: Enterprise Standard, and PlusEducation: Education PlusConsumer: Google AI Pro and UltraEducation Add-ons: Google AI Pro for Education; Teaching and Learning

            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're an Android user who is seeing ads pop up after your phone calls, you need not assume this is some new feature you have to learn to live with. It's actually an ad fraud scam, and you can do something about it. Researchers have identified dozens of apps on the Google Play Store that are able to display ads on top of the Android phone interface, a scheme known as AfterCall. How ads are taking over Android callsThis scam originates with seemingly harmless utility apps downloaded from the Google Play Store, such as calendars, alarm clocks, and notepads. When installed, they request overlay permissions, which allow them to appear on top of other apps—and thus display ads over phone calls. These apps can detect when a call ends and will then launch full-screen ads wrapped in a fake call info screen. Since it looks like they are simply part of the call interface, users may be less likely to suspect that they are actually malicious. It's worth noting that overlay permissions can't be granted via a standard pop-up during the app installation process. They are a type of "special permission" that requires users to go into their system settings to enable. Android apps are supposed to request these permissions in context and give a clear reason for doing so. AfterCall scammers are using justifications like alarms not being able to go off or appear correctly without overlay permissions, though some apps will simply crash if users decline permissions.
How to remove AfterCall adsBecause the ads appear out of context—after a phone call and with content unrelated to the utility app—it's harder for users to figure out what's causing them. The utility apps aren't obviously malicious and don't appear on recent app lists when ads are displayed, so it's not obvious that they are connected to the problem. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you are seeing ads pop up after phone calls on your Android, check for apps that have overlay permissions. Go to Settings > Apps > Special app access (this may be hidden behind a three-dot menu) and click on the permission type. Look for apps you don't recognize, or which shouldn't have "display on top" permissions, and uninstall them. You should regularly audit these permissions, and disable any that aren't essential. On the user side, these apps seem to be mostly an annoyance rather than outright malicious programs that are harvesting your sensitive data, though installing any program that requests unnecessary permissions can introduce significant risk. If nothing else, however, these apps do appear to waste brands' advertising dollars and could damage their reputation with users—but you probably just care about how to stop seeing them after your calls.

        Apple just released the second public betas of both iOS 27 and macOS 27—only a week after the launch of public beta 1—so anyone signed up for the beta program can now test the latest public version of the software on their compatible iPhones and Macs. The biggest features coming to iOS 27 and macOS 27 are related to Siri AI, Apple Intelligence tools, and Liquid Glass customizations, as well as performance upgrades; so if you don't want to wait until the full release in the fall to try these out, you can install the public betas as they become available. iOS 27 and macOS 27 public beta 2 updatesLast week, Apple released iOS 27 and macOS beta 4 for developers, which 9to5Mac notes are the same build as public beta 2. While the macOS 27 update seems to be mostly bug fixes and small improvements to performance and stability, the latest developer release for iOS 27 did introduce some more substantive changes. 
For example, Siri has several additional voice options, and there's a new splash screen for Siri AI that explains its features when users open it for the first time. There's an adaptive mode slider for AirPods Pro in the Control Center, and the TV app will automatically download upcoming episodes for shows you are watching and remove downloads to manage storage space. You can also adjust how much text is previewed in chat lists, and "Zoom Photos to Fill" allows images to automatically fill your device's display. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Anyone with a compatible device can try Apple's public betas—you'll just need to enroll your Apple Account in Apple's beta program. We've covered the process for both iOS 27 and macOS 27, including which devices can run the update and the potential risks involved with installing a public beta. While public betas are typically safer than developer betas, they're not perfect, and it's always possible that bugs will slip through. At the very least, you'll want to make sure you have a backup of your data, just in case.

title: You Can Now Verify Your Facebook Account With a Video Selfie
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C.             Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Facebook is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark.
                                            This is a separate feature from Meta Verified, which is a paid subscription for obtaining a blue check mark in Facebook and Instagram.
                                            You'll record a short selfie video, which Facebook will compare to other profile photos, but you should consider whether you want to provide more data to Meta.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're on Facebook, you may soon see a new type of verification badge on user profiles meant to indicate that there is a real, live person behind them. The platform is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark, which will appear on their profile and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. (At launch, badges won't appear in Feed posts, but Facebook says that feature will be added in the future.)Note that this is different from Meta Verified, a paid subscription that provides the blue check mark to accounts on Facebook and Instagram. This verification indicates that Meta has confirmed the user's identity based on a review of their government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video. How Facebook Verified worksFacebook Verified is available to users age 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with the platform's community standards, though the feature is launching in select markets initially before being rolled out globally. Once you have access, you'll need to record a short video selfie, which Facebook will compare to existing profile photos on your account using facial recognition. If your verification is approved, the white check mark will be added to your profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts. 
Consider your privacy firstFacebook says it will store your selfie video for "up to 30 days" after verification, which is a one-time process. It's not entirely clear what happens with that video in the meantime, and it's worth noting that Meta has relied on user data to train its AI. Meta AI (and Meta more broadly) is a terrible offender when it comes to privacy and security, so you should consider whether the tradeoff of a verification mark is worth handing over more of your data and read the privacy policy before you agree. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Google also launched a video selfie verification feature this week, though its purpose is to prove your identity should you get locked out of your account. Unlike Facebook Verified, which is meant to be a trust signal to other users, Google's selfie verification allows access to your entire Google account, bringing with it some additional security considerations.

title: How Apple Might Try to Make Its Smart Glasses Less Creepy
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 27, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Drop of Light/Shutterstock
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple's first line of smart glasses are expected in 2027.
                                            The company is reportedly mulling a camera that's just used for AI, with no way for users to take pictures.
                                            Apple's issue reflects an industry wide concern over privacy implications of camera-armed smart glasses.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple is expected to reveal its smart glasses, codename N50, at WWDC 17 in June 2027, which gives the company nearly a year to wrestle with the thorniest problem facing smart glasses: how do you uphold a commitment to privacy while selling a product that contains a hidden camera?Like industry leader Meta's line of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses, Apple's first smart glasses are expected to focus on AI, audio, and onboard cameras (display models are expected at a later date.) But Meta's glasses are at the center of a growing cultural firestorm for the camera feature, with people calling Metas "pervert glasses," creating guerrilla marketing campaigns against them, and banning them from a growing number of locations. According to a Bloomberg report from Mark Gurman, Apple is considering releasing smart glasses with a full camera system that can't be used to take pictures or record video. The camera system would be used only for feeding visual information to Apple's AI tools, with no way for users to share that information. 
Apple's commitment to privacyPrivacy (either respecting or exploiting) is no doubt at the forefront of every smart glass manufacturer's design decisions, but it's a particularly thorny issue for Apple, given its carefully cultivated image as "privacy first" company. Apple has spent years making data security a pillar of its identity, whether by repeatedly publicly proclaiming it as a "fundamental human right" or stressing on-device processing. Releasing a pair of glasses many would regard as spy glasses could effectively undermine Apple's reputation, even if every other privacy option (no sharing content with third parties, as much on-device processing as possible, etc.) is as robust as possible.This isn't the first time Apple has been here. When it launched AirTags in 2021, the company built in anti-stalking features like unwanted-tracker alerts, audible chirps, and tools to locate a hidden tag, all to prevent the device from being used to secretly monitor people. But within months, the devices were reported in stalking and domestic abuse cases, prompting lawsuits, news investigations, and the general view of AirTags as tools for creeps. The lesson: good intentions and good engineering are no match for people's worst instincts. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
According to consumer research, taking quick videos and pictures is one of the primary reasons people are buying smart glasses in the first place: a February 2026 Counterpoint Research report highlights that enhanced video performance and photography are the most frequently praised features of the Gen 2 Meta glasses. If consumers are facing a decision between Meta glasses, soon-to-be-released Samsung/Google smart glasses, and Apple glasses, how many would choose the one that doesn't have a camera?Other possible privacy solutions for smart glassesWhile I have no idea what other possible solutions to the privacy problem Apple is considering, if I had to guess, I'd say they've discussed these ideas:Geofencing: Apple could proactively build geofencing or detection agreements with categories of space like courts, gyms, and schools, or provide some kind of opt-in "fence" for users, like an iPhone setting for "no hidden cameras within my home/business." Given the ban of camera glasses in specific places like New York courts and sections of cruise ships, this seems like a strong contender for where things are headed. Highly visible status light: Some of the backlash Meta has faced for its camera glasses is over the size of its tiny "I'm taping" warning light. What if it was bigger, brighter, and more visible? I could see that satisfying some people that don't wear and don't like smart glasses with cameras, but how many users want to advertise that they're wearing smart glasses? A warning system for non-glasses users:  There is already an app that tries to warn users if a pair of Meta glasses is in the vicinity; Apple could take the same idea and make it easy for anyone who cares to see who is wearing a pair of Apple glasses around them. Maybe this would even work as advertising, although again, I doubt glasses wearers would like to be singled out like this. Count on this to blow over: Apple may decide it doesn't care about privacy that much after all; it wouldn't be the first time a company ditched a core value in favor of making a lot of money. Since there's more than a year until Apple glasses are expected to hit shelves, the company might just hope for the best. Public attitudes tend to get less alarmist over time as more people get used to new technology; when camera-equipped cell phones hit the market in the early 2000s, there was widespread panic over photography in gym locker rooms and schools, but that's not something anyone worries as much about these days.

title: You Can Now Let Gemini 'See' Your Mac's Display for Free
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 29, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Gemini's latest update for macOS adds two new features, one of which is less straightforward than the other.
                                            The first improves dictation, removing the "ums" and "ahs" from your speech.
                                            The second lets Gemini see everything you do on your computer, so it can perform more complex tasks on your behalf.
                                            It's not a true agentic feature, but it could come with some privacy and security risks.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It may be polarizing, but there are lot of people using AI right now. Most of those users are likely exclusive to a chatbot, like ChatGPT or Gemini, using it as a Google replacement (don't do that), or as a confidant (please don't do that either). But if your goal is to use AI as a personal assistant, listen up: On Wednesday, Google announced two new updates for Gemini on macOS, one of which may have some privacy and security implications for users—assuming they opt in to it. Gemini on macOS gets enhanced dictationIf you use dictation on macOS (i.e., speaking words out loud and having the AI type them for you), you might have a reason to use Gemini over Apple's built-in solutions. Going forward, Gemini on macOS has "intelligent dictation," which Google says polishes text "instantly at the cursor." That means Gemini will remove your stammers, like "ums" and "ahs" in between words, things you never would type out yourself. This works in any window on your Mac: You just press the Fn key, and start speaking. We'll have to see this feature in action to know how well it works, but it does build off of similar enhancements Gemini has on other platforms. It's a small adjustment, but one that will make it possible to use Gemini to draft texts, emails, or documents without having to totally self-edit. That's the kind of utility I'm looking for from AI features. And since it's enabled by default, everyone using Gemini on Mac will be using it—unless they dig into their settings to turn it off.
Google's second update for Gemini on macOS isn't so straightforward, nor is it enabled by default. Google calls it "screen-aware reasoning," a feature that grants Gemini permission to "understand" what's happening on your Mac's screen. The idea is to hand tasks over to Gemini: If you have your Notes app open, for example, you could press the Fn key and say "Turn these notes into an executive summary for the meeting this afternoon." Gemini will reportedly know to look at your Notes app, analyze your text, and configure it on your behalf, all without needing to work through a proprietary app. You can stack together a series of commands, too: You could ask Gemini to draft an email for a team dinner, and pull from a select group of files on your Mac for important info (participants, budget requirements, dietary restrictions, etc.) You could continue on, asking Gemini to search Google Maps for specific types of restaurants, and include them as options for the team. And at any point, you can correct yourself, and Gemini will adjust accordingly. For example, if you said the team dinner should be at 6:30 p.m. on Friday, but later on in your command you say, "Sorry, dinner should be 7 p.m." Gemini should make the appropriate changes.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Sure, there's a usefulness to this type of feature. If you're already using Gemini on macOS, letting "see" your Mac's display makes it more helpful. Rather than rely on the Gemini app for all your tasks, you can expand its range to your whole Mac, and, if Google is correct, in quite a complex way. But there's always a privacy risk in allowing AI programs full access to what's happening on your personal computer, and perhaps a security risk as well. Do you want Google's AI to be able to see everything on your screen? It's not as big a risk as a true agentic program, of course. If you pay for Google's most expensive AI plan, you can access Gemini Spark, which can run autonomously on your Mac. The biggest flag to note is "prompt injection," in which hackers hide malicious commands for your AI in websites. If you task the AI to do something, and it stumbles upon such a command, it will think the request comes from you, not from the hacker. So, when it processes a request like "open [malicious site] and download [malicious file]" it will without question; or "open [crypto wallet], log in with saved credentials, and send funds to [account]," it will follow suit. That shouldn't be an issue with Gemini as it stands, though it theoretically could, if you ask it to perform a task that exposes it to prompt injection.  If you're someone who is interested in the latest features, this isn't to dissuade you from using Gemini's new agentic feature on macOS, but it's worth considering the very real risks before you do.

title: No, Bananas Don't Destroy the Nutrients in Smoothies
description: Who doesn't love a banana in their smoothie? It adds sweetness and does wonders for the texture. Well, not Rhonda Patrick, who proud
body:
Who doesn't love a banana in their smoothie? It adds sweetness and does wonders for the texture. Well, not Rhonda Patrick, who proudly told her followers she does not put bananas in her smoothies because of a fear that it's breaking down polyphenols from blueberries. This belief is one that made the rounds on social media a few years ago, and its grain of truth has been blown way out of proportion. I'll break down where this myth comes from, and what you actually need to know. Why people believe bananas are bad for smoothiesThe idea that you need to avoid bananas in your smoothies started in 2023, when a study published in the journal Food & Function found that bananas can reduce the bioavailability of flavon-3-ols in smoothies. The study is real, and several of the TikTok clips that immediately popped up to discuss it described the study more or less accurately. Where they went wrong is concluding that we shouldn’t put bananas in our smoothies. That’s not what the scientists concluded. There’s no need to give up your bananas. The press release announcing the study probably started this mess (it calls adding a banana to your smoothie a “mistake”) but it also mentions that the lead author of the study, Javier Ottaviani, “said bananas remain a great fruit to be eaten or consumed in smoothies.” So clearly the banana warnings are overblown. What the study actually foundThe study wasn’t about the nutritional value of bananas or smoothies in general. It was looking at a particular question of biochemistry: Does an enzyme in bananas react with one particular type of antioxidant found in cocoa extract? (Note that Rhonda Patrick's recent videos are focused  on polyphenols in blueberries; those weren't tested in the study.)Antioxidants are a broad class of chemicals. For context, vitamin C is an antioxidant, but so are lycopene and resveratrol (compounds famously found in tomatoes and grapes) and so are anthocyanins, the red and blue pigments found in berries. The antioxidant studied here is not any of the above, but a different one found in tea and cocoa. It’s called (-)-epicatechin, and it’s part of the antioxidant family called flavon-3-ols. In the study, eight healthy men recruited from around the UC Davis campus were given each of the following, on different days: A smoothie made with bananas, almond milk, and an epicatechin-containing cocoa extract.A smoothie made with the same cocoa extract plus strawberries, blueberries, blackberries, raspberries, almond milk, water, crushed ice, and yogurt (presumably the yogurt and ice were required for texture).A glass of milk and a capsule containing the cocoa extract.Bananas contain an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase (PPO), and the scientists wanted to find out if the PPO in a banana could affect the levels of (-)-epicatechin, one of those flavon-3-ols, in food such as smoothies.Somewhat surprisingly, it did! Our bodies convert epicatechins into other chemicals in the same family, and the researchers took blood samples from the volunteers to look for these chemicals after each of the experiments. After drinking the berry smoothie or taking the capsule with milk, blood levels of these chemicals were elevated. But after drinking the banana smoothie, they weren’t. This strongly suggests that the PPO in the banana had destroyed a lot of the epicatechins present in the cocoa extract. Further experiments described in same paper suggest that this chemical activity happens when the ingredients are sitting together in the smoothie glass, and it likely also happens in our stomachs. More importantly, what the study did not findThe study did not test a berry smoothie with an added banana. None of the smoothies or experiments combined berries and bananas. The study did not test levels of antioxidants or other nutrients from berries. They were looking specifically at what happened to the antioxidants provided in the cocoa extract. The study also did not look at other aspects of nutrition besides this very specific chemical reaction (PPO from bananas plus (-)-epicatechins from cocoa extract). 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Therefore, we cannot conclude that the banana in a mixed fruit smoothie “destroys” or “ruins” the nutrients or even the antioxidants from the berries. This is a study about a specific type of polyphenol that's found in tea and cocoa, and it was studied specifically in a cocoa extract. We can't use this data to say what happens to the antioxidants in berries. Why you can’t really “destroy” nutrition, anywayIf an enzyme in bananas can reduce the bioavailability of a certain family of antioxidants...what does that matter? Were you drinking smoothies for the express purpose of increasing your intake of flavon-3-ols? More likely you were trying to get some fruit in your diet and/or have a nice breakfast or snack because you were hungry. Regardless of their PPO activity, bananas also provide fiber, which is good for you, and carbs, which are a macronutrient our bodies can use in many ways. A medium banana contains 20% of our vitamin B6 needs for the day, 17% of our vitamin C, and 8% of our magnesium. After getting backlash about the banana myth, Patrick made a video in which she points out that bananas also have more sugar than avocados (her preferred ingredient). That's a plus, in my opinion: A smoothie needs some sweetness, and carbs are good for you anyway.The recent study did not take any of that away from you. You still get all of the benefits above, no matter what’s happening to the flavon-3-ols in your smoothie.If you’re really worried about your flavon-3-ols, there’s a better solution than giving up bananasOK, but what if you really were looking forward to getting lots of good antioxidants in that fruit smoothie? After all, flavon-3-ols like (-)-epicatechin are so good for us that the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (AND) issued a guideline for them, even though flavon-3-ols are a non-essential nutrient. The guideline tells us that there are heath benefits to be gained by consuming at least 400 milligrams of flavon-3-ols per day. If you want to get more flavon-3-ols, the best thing you can do is drink some tea. You can hit that 400-milligram recommendation with just 10 ounces of green tea (two small cups), or 12 ounces of black tea. There are flavon-3-ols in berries, but in lesser amounts; it would take 6 cups of blackberries or 40 cups of blueberries to provide the same amount as those two cups of green tea. By the way, the same AND paper that recommended 400 milligrams of flavon-3-ols says it’s best not to get this nutrient from supplements. That’s because the most common supplements to provide it are green tea extracts, and green tea extracts can cause stomach upset and even be toxic to your liver in large amounts.
